Manuscripts of the Mahabharata, Rajatarangini and Arthashastra join UNESCO's Asia-Pacific memory register

Three Sanskrit manuscripts held in Pune, Mysuru and Srinagar were inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Asia-Pacific Regional Register at a meeting in Jakarta, taking India's entries on that register to six.

Talaash Heritage desk · Published 12 November 2026

Where
Pune, Mysuru and Srinagar

Three Indian manuscripts have been added to the Memory of the World Regional Register for Asia and the Pacific, kept by UNESCO's regional committee for the programme (MOWCAP). The decision was taken at the committee's 11th session in Jakarta, Indonesia, and the government's PIB Culture account announced it on X on 5 November 2026. The Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA) prepared the nomination dossiers for all three.

The first is a birch-bark manuscript of the Mahabharata at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune. ThePrint reports that the Indologist Georg Bühler acquired it in Kashmir in 1875, and that it preserves the old Kashmiri version of the epic.

The second is a complete 16th-century palm-leaf manuscript of Kautilya's Arthashastra, the Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, government and economy, written in the Grantha script and held at the Oriental Research Institute in Mysuru.

The third is a manuscript of Kalhana's Rajatarangini, the verse chronicle of the kings of Kashmir that Kalhana composed in Sanskrit around 1148 to 1149 CE. It is kept at the Oriental Research Library in the Sri Pratap Singh Library Complex, Srinagar.

Rising Kashmir and India News Network report that the three bring India's entries on this regional register to six. The earlier three, inscribed in 2024, are illustrated manuscripts of the Ramcharitmanas, a 15th-century manuscript of the Panchatantra and a manuscript of the Sahrdayaloka-Locana. The regional register is separate from UNESCO's International Memory of the World Register, on which the Natyashastra and the Bhagavad Gita were inscribed in April 2025.
